case_info.scenario: A man in his mid-50s with a medical history of nonspecific T-wave abnormalities on electrocardiogram (ECG) reported new-onset chest discomfort, diaphoresis, and shortness of breath that woke him from sleep. Emergency medical services found him to be in a wide complex tachycardia. He was administered a 150-mg bolus of intravenous amiodarone, which failed to terminate his arrhythmia. He ultimately required synchronized cardioversion with a biphasic direct current shock of 100 J. On arrival to the emergency department, his vital signs were stable. Serum electrolyte levels were within normal range and C-reactive protein was less than 6 mg/dL (to convert to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10). High-sensitivity troponin peaked at 1078 pg/mL. His initial 12-lead ECG is shown inFigure 1A. He continued in sinus rhythm with episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia observed on telemetry, as shown inFigure 1B. Cardiac catheterization revealed patent coronary arteries. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was remarkable for a dilated right ventricle with moderately reduced systolic function and transmural late gadolinium enhancement with akinesis and dyskinesis involving the right ventricular (RV) free wall and outflow tract extending to the left ventricular (LV) anterior, septal, and apical segments.

case_info.caption: Electrocardiogram (ECG) and telemetry. A, Twelve-lead ECG on arrival to the emergency department. B, Nonsustained ventricular tachycardia on telemetry.
case_info.explanation: B. Cardiac positron emission tomography Several ECG features suggest a diagnosis of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) in this case. There is a notable low-amplitude, positive deflection between the end of the QRS complex and the onset of the T wave, most prominent in the right precordial leads (V2 and V3), consistent with an epsilon wave. Other findings include both premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with a left bundle branch block (LBBB) morphology and an inferior axis. T-wave inversions are seen in leads V1-V4, though notably in the presence of a complete right bundle branch block (cRBBB). The patient met diagnostic criteria for ARVC based on electrophysiological data alone: 1 major criterion, ie, presence of epsilon waves on the ECGs, and 3 minor criteria including T-wave inversions in V1-V4 in the presence of cRBBB, frequent PVCs (>500 per 24 hours on telemetry), as well as nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with an LBBB morphology.1The diagnosis of ARVC was further supported by major imaging criteria as cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed RV regional akinesis and dyskinesis, RV end diastolic volume more than 110 mL/m2, and a moderately decreased systolic function with ejection fraction of 40% or less.1Notably, there was also significant LV involvement with late gadolinium enhancement composing 38% of total LV myocardial mass. However, this finding does not necessarily raise doubt with respect to a diagnosis of ARVC, as concomitant involvement of the left ventricle is a well-documented feature of advanced ARVC, with 1 study documenting LV involvement in 76% of hearts with autopsy-proven ARVC.2 Despite meeting diagnostic criteria for ARVC, there was considerable debate about the underlying pathology given the initial ECG with a “normal” first beat, in which the absence of cRBBB was accompanied by disappearance of T-wave inversion in lead V1 (Figure 1A). In other words, T-wave inversion seen in the right precordial leads, the most frequent ECG abnormality observed in ARVC,1may simply be secondary to conduction delay from cRBBB in the present case. Additionally, although the presence of epsilon waves in the right precordial leads is a major diagnostic criterion, this finding alone is not pathognomonic of ARVC. An epsilon wave is an electrical marker of delayed activation of the right ventricular free wall and outflow tract and can be seen in association with other cardiac pathologies that involve the right ventricle such as myocardial infarction and sarcoidosis.3Myocarditis may also be associated with epsilon waves,4though this patient’s inflammatory markers including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were undetectably low, strongly favoring against active myocarditis. With regard to the best next step in management, an echocardiogram is limited in its ability to definitively evaluate for major imaging features necessary to discern a diagnosis of ARVC vs cardiac sarcoidosis (choice C). An electrophysiology study would be premature and unlikely to aid in establishing an etiology (choice D). Discharge home after implantation of implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (choice A) would also be incorrect at this point because the medical management of ARVC and cardiac sarcoidosis is considerably different. Cardiac 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (Figure 2) scan was obtained (choice B), which showed focal/multifocal FDG uptake in the myocardium as well as in the lung and intrathoracic and abdominal lymph nodes, suggestive of active myocardial and systemic sarcoidosis. The patient underwent placement of an implantable cardiac defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death. He was discharged receiving guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and started receiving prednisone with plans for a prolonged taper for active systemic and cardiac sarcoidosis. In the outpatient setting, he underwent genetic testing for ARVC, which was negative for a pathogenic mutation.

The combination of RV/LV involvement with transmural LGE and ventricular arrhythmias in a patient with normal coronaries strongly points to cardiac sarcoidosis or another infiltrative cardiomyopathy. Discharging immediately after ICD placement without confirming the underlying etiology and starting targeted immunosuppressive therapy could leave a reversible condition untreated.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: B. Cardiac positron emission tomography Several ECG features suggest a diagnosis of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) in this case. There is a notable low-amplitude, positive deflection between the end of the QRS complex and the onset of the T wave, most prominent in the right precordial leads (V2 and V3), consistent with an epsilon wave. Other findings include both premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with a left bundle branch block (LBBB) morphology and an inferior axis. T-wave inversions are seen in leads V1-V4, though notably in the presence of a complete right bundle branch block (cRBBB). The patient met diagnostic criteria for ARVC based on electrophysiological data alone: 1 major criterion, ie, presence of epsilon waves on the ECGs, and 3 minor criteria including T-wave inversions in V1-V4 in the presence of cRBBB, frequent PVCs (>500 per 24 hours on telemetry), as well as nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with an LBBB morphology.1The diagnosis of ARVC was further supported by major imaging criteria as cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed RV regional akinesis and dyskinesis, RV end diastolic volume more than 110 mL/m2, and a moderately decreased systolic function with ejection fraction of 40% or less.1Notably, there was also significant LV involvement with late gadolinium enhancement composing 38% of total LV myocardial mass. However, this finding does not necessarily raise doubt with respect to a diagnosis of ARVC, as concomitant involvement of the left ventricle is a well-documented feature of advanced ARVC, with 1 study documenting LV involvement in 76% of hearts with autopsy-proven ARVC.2 Despite meeting diagnostic criteria for ARVC, there was considerable debate about the underlying pathology given the initial ECG with a “normal” first beat, in which the absence of cRBBB was accompanied by disappearance of T-wave inversion in lead V1 (Figure 1A). In other words, T-wave inversion seen in the right precordial leads, the most frequent ECG abnormality observed in ARVC,1may simply be secondary to conduction delay from cRBBB in the present case. Additionally, although the presence of epsilon waves in the right precordial leads is a major diagnostic criterion, this finding alone is not pathognomonic of ARVC. An epsilon wave is an electrical marker of delayed activation of the right ventricular free wall and outflow tract and can be seen in association with other cardiac pathologies that involve the right ventricle such as myocardial infarction and sarcoidosis.3Myocarditis may also be associated with epsilon waves,4though this patient’s inflammatory markers including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were undetectably low, strongly favoring against active myocarditis. With regard to the best next step in management, an echocardiogram is limited in its ability to definitively evaluate for major imaging features necessary to discern a diagnosis of ARVC vs cardiac sarcoidosis (choice C). An electrophysiology study would be premature and unlikely to aid in establishing an etiology (choice D). Discharge home after implantation of implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (choice A) would also be incorrect at this point because the medical management of ARVC and cardiac sarcoidosis is considerably different. Cardiac 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (Figure 2) scan was obtained (choice B), which showed focal/multifocal FDG uptake in the myocardium as well as in the lung and intrathoracic and abdominal lymph nodes, suggestive of active myocardial and systemic sarcoidosis. The patient underwent placement of an implantable cardiac defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death. He was discharged receiving guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and started receiving prednisone with plans for a prolonged taper for active systemic and cardiac sarcoidosis. In the outpatient setting, he underwent genetic testing for ARVC, which was negative for a pathogenic mutation.

      not by analogy to the others.

1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.

     after the AI's message.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."

case_info.explanation: B. Cardiac positron emission tomography Several ECG features suggest a diagnosis of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) in this case. There is a notable low-amplitude, positive deflection between the end of the QRS complex and the onset of the T wave, most prominent in the right precordial leads (V2 and V3), consistent with an epsilon wave. Other findings include both premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with a left bundle branch block (LBBB) morphology and an inferior axis. T-wave inversions are seen in leads V1-V4, though notably in the presence of a complete right bundle branch block (cRBBB). The patient met diagnostic criteria for ARVC based on electrophysiological data alone: 1 major criterion, ie, presence of epsilon waves on the ECGs, and 3 minor criteria including T-wave inversions in V1-V4 in the presence of cRBBB, frequent PVCs (>500 per 24 hours on telemetry), as well as nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with an LBBB morphology.1The diagnosis of ARVC was further supported by major imaging criteria as cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed RV regional akinesis and dyskinesis, RV end diastolic volume more than 110 mL/m2, and a moderately decreased systolic function with ejection fraction of 40% or less.1Notably, there was also significant LV involvement with late gadolinium enhancement composing 38% of total LV myocardial mass. However, this finding does not necessarily raise doubt with respect to a diagnosis of ARVC, as concomitant involvement of the left ventricle is a well-documented feature of advanced ARVC, with 1 study documenting LV involvement in 76% of hearts with autopsy-proven ARVC.2 Despite meeting diagnostic criteria for ARVC, there was considerable debate about the underlying pathology given the initial ECG with a “normal” first beat, in which the absence of cRBBB was accompanied by disappearance of T-wave inversion in lead V1 (Figure 1A). In other words, T-wave inversion seen in the right precordial leads, the most frequent ECG abnormality observed in ARVC,1may simply be secondary to conduction delay from cRBBB in the present case. Additionally, although the presence of epsilon waves in the right precordial leads is a major diagnostic criterion, this finding alone is not pathognomonic of ARVC. An epsilon wave is an electrical marker of delayed activation of the right ventricular free wall and outflow tract and can be seen in association with other cardiac pathologies that involve the right ventricle such as myocardial infarction and sarcoidosis.3Myocarditis may also be associated with epsilon waves,4though this patient’s inflammatory markers including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were undetectably low, strongly favoring against active myocarditis. With regard to the best next step in management, an echocardiogram is limited in its ability to definitively evaluate for major imaging features necessary to discern a diagnosis of ARVC vs cardiac sarcoidosis (choice C). An electrophysiology study would be premature and unlikely to aid in establishing an etiology (choice D). Discharge home after implantation of implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (choice A) would also be incorrect at this point because the medical management of ARVC and cardiac sarcoidosis is considerably different. Cardiac 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (Figure 2) scan was obtained (choice B), which showed focal/multifocal FDG uptake in the myocardium as well as in the lung and intrathoracic and abdominal lymph nodes, suggestive of active myocardial and systemic sarcoidosis. The patient underwent placement of an implantable cardiac defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death. He was discharged receiving guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and started receiving prednisone with plans for a prolonged taper for active systemic and cardiac sarcoidosis. In the outpatient setting, he underwent genetic testing for ARVC, which was negative for a pathogenic mutation.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an

case_info.explanation: B. Cardiac positron emission tomography Several ECG features suggest a diagnosis of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) in this case. There is a notable low-amplitude, positive deflection between the end of the QRS complex and the onset of the T wave, most prominent in the right precordial leads (V2 and V3), consistent with an epsilon wave. Other findings include both premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with a left bundle branch block (LBBB) morphology and an inferior axis. T-wave inversions are seen in leads V1-V4, though notably in the presence of a complete right bundle branch block (cRBBB). The patient met diagnostic criteria for ARVC based on electrophysiological data alone: 1 major criterion, ie, presence of epsilon waves on the ECGs, and 3 minor criteria including T-wave inversions in V1-V4 in the presence of cRBBB, frequent PVCs (>500 per 24 hours on telemetry), as well as nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with an LBBB morphology.1The diagnosis of ARVC was further supported by major imaging criteria as cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed RV regional akinesis and dyskinesis, RV end diastolic volume more than 110 mL/m2, and a moderately decreased systolic function with ejection fraction of 40% or less.1Notably, there was also significant LV involvement with late gadolinium enhancement composing 38% of total LV myocardial mass. However, this finding does not necessarily raise doubt with respect to a diagnosis of ARVC, as concomitant involvement of the left ventricle is a well-documented feature of advanced ARVC, with 1 study documenting LV involvement in 76% of hearts with autopsy-proven ARVC.2 Despite meeting diagnostic criteria for ARVC, there was considerable debate about the underlying pathology given the initial ECG with a “normal” first beat, in which the absence of cRBBB was accompanied by disappearance of T-wave inversion in lead V1 (Figure 1A). In other words, T-wave inversion seen in the right precordial leads, the most frequent ECG abnormality observed in ARVC,1may simply be secondary to conduction delay from cRBBB in the present case. Additionally, although the presence of epsilon waves in the right precordial leads is a major diagnostic criterion, this finding alone is not pathognomonic of ARVC. An epsilon wave is an electrical marker of delayed activation of the right ventricular free wall and outflow tract and can be seen in association with other cardiac pathologies that involve the right ventricle such as myocardial infarction and sarcoidosis.3Myocarditis may also be associated with epsilon waves,4though this patient’s inflammatory markers including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were undetectably low, strongly favoring against active myocarditis. With regard to the best next step in management, an echocardiogram is limited in its ability to definitively evaluate for major imaging features necessary to discern a diagnosis of ARVC vs cardiac sarcoidosis (choice C). An electrophysiology study would be premature and unlikely to aid in establishing an etiology (choice D). Discharge home after implantation of implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (choice A) would also be incorrect at this point because the medical management of ARVC and cardiac sarcoidosis is considerably different. Cardiac 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (Figure 2) scan was obtained (choice B), which showed focal/multifocal FDG uptake in the myocardium as well as in the lung and intrathoracic and abdominal lymph nodes, suggestive of active myocardial and systemic sarcoidosis. The patient underwent placement of an implantable cardiac defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death. He was discharged receiving guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and started receiving prednisone with plans for a prolonged taper for active systemic and cardiac sarcoidosis. In the outpatient setting, he underwent genetic testing for ARVC, which was negative for a pathogenic mutation.

case_info.explanation: B. Cardiac positron emission tomography Several ECG features suggest a diagnosis of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) in this case. There is a notable low-amplitude, positive deflection between the end of the QRS complex and the onset of the T wave, most prominent in the right precordial leads (V2 and V3), consistent with an epsilon wave. Other findings include both premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with a left bundle branch block (LBBB) morphology and an inferior axis. T-wave inversions are seen in leads V1-V4, though notably in the presence of a complete right bundle branch block (cRBBB). The patient met diagnostic criteria for ARVC based on electrophysiological data alone: 1 major criterion, ie, presence of epsilon waves on the ECGs, and 3 minor criteria including T-wave inversions in V1-V4 in the presence of cRBBB, frequent PVCs (>500 per 24 hours on telemetry), as well as nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with an LBBB morphology.1The diagnosis of ARVC was further supported by major imaging criteria as cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed RV regional akinesis and dyskinesis, RV end diastolic volume more than 110 mL/m2, and a moderately decreased systolic function with ejection fraction of 40% or less.1Notably, there was also significant LV involvement with late gadolinium enhancement composing 38% of total LV myocardial mass. However, this finding does not necessarily raise doubt with respect to a diagnosis of ARVC, as concomitant involvement of the left ventricle is a well-documented feature of advanced ARVC, with 1 study documenting LV involvement in 76% of hearts with autopsy-proven ARVC.2 Despite meeting diagnostic criteria for ARVC, there was considerable debate about the underlying pathology given the initial ECG with a “normal” first beat, in which the absence of cRBBB was accompanied by disappearance of T-wave inversion in lead V1 (Figure 1A). In other words, T-wave inversion seen in the right precordial leads, the most frequent ECG abnormality observed in ARVC,1may simply be secondary to conduction delay from cRBBB in the present case. Additionally, although the presence of epsilon waves in the right precordial leads is a major diagnostic criterion, this finding alone is not pathognomonic of ARVC. An epsilon wave is an electrical marker of delayed activation of the right ventricular free wall and outflow tract and can be seen in association with other cardiac pathologies that involve the right ventricle such as myocardial infarction and sarcoidosis.3Myocarditis may also be associated with epsilon waves,4though this patient’s inflammatory markers including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were undetectably low, strongly favoring against active myocarditis. With regard to the best next step in management, an echocardiogram is limited in its ability to definitively evaluate for major imaging features necessary to discern a diagnosis of ARVC vs cardiac sarcoidosis (choice C). An electrophysiology study would be premature and unlikely to aid in establishing an etiology (choice D). Discharge home after implantation of implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (choice A) would also be incorrect at this point because the medical management of ARVC and cardiac sarcoidosis is considerably different. Cardiac 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (Figure 2) scan was obtained (choice B), which showed focal/multifocal FDG uptake in the myocardium as well as in the lung and intrathoracic and abdominal lymph nodes, suggestive of active myocardial and systemic sarcoidosis. The patient underwent placement of an implantable cardiac defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death. He was discharged receiving guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and started receiving prednisone with plans for a prolonged taper for active systemic and cardiac sarcoidosis. [NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: B. Cardiac positron emission tomography Several ECG features suggest a diagnosis of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) in this case. There is a notable low-amplitude, positive deflection between the end of the QRS complex and the onset of the T wave, most prominent in the right precordial leads (V2 and V3), consistent with an epsilon wave. Other findings include both premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with a left bundle branch block (LBBB) morphology and an inferior axis. T-wave inversions are seen in leads V1-V4, though notably in the presence of a complete right bundle branch block (cRBBB). The patient met diagnostic criteria for ARVC based on electrophysiological data alone: 1 major criterion, ie, presence of epsilon waves on the ECGs, and 3 minor criteria including T-wave inversions in V1-V4 in the presence of cRBBB, frequent PVCs (>500 per 24 hours on telemetry), as well as nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with an LBBB morphology.1The diagnosis of ARVC was further supported by major imaging criteria as cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed RV regional akinesis and dyskinesis, RV end diastolic volume more than 110 mL/m2, and a moderately decreased systolic function with ejection fraction of 40% or less.1Notably, there was also significant LV involvement with late gadolinium enhancement composing 38% of total LV myocardial mass. However, this finding does not necessarily raise doubt with respect to a diagnosis of ARVC, as concomitant involvement of the left ventricle is a well-documented feature of advanced ARVC, with 1 study documenting LV involvement in 76% of hearts with autopsy-proven ARVC.2 Despite meeting diagnostic criteria for ARVC, there was considerable debate about the underlying pathology given the initial ECG with a “normal” first beat, in which the absence of cRBBB was accompanied by disappearance of T-wave inversion in lead V1 (Figure 1A). In other words, T-wave inversion seen in the right precordial leads, the most frequent ECG abnormality observed in ARVC,1may simply be secondary to conduction delay from cRBBB in the present case. Additionally, although the presence of epsilon waves in the right precordial leads is a major diagnostic criterion, this finding alone is not pathognomonic of ARVC. An epsilon wave is an electrical marker of delayed activation of the right ventricular free wall and outflow tract and can be seen in association with other cardiac pathologies that involve the right ventricle such as myocardial infarction and sarcoidosis.3Myocarditis may also be associated with epsilon waves,4though this patient’s inflammatory markers including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were undetectably low, strongly favoring against active myocarditis. With regard to the best next step in management, an echocardiogram is limited in its ability to definitively evaluate for major imaging features necessary to discern a diagnosis of ARVC vs cardiac sarcoidosis (choice C). An electrophysiology study would be premature and unlikely to aid in establishing an etiology (choice D). Discharge home after implantation of implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (choice A) would also be incorrect at this point because the medical management of ARVC and cardiac sarcoidosis is considerably different. Cardiac 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (Figure 2) scan was obtained (choice B), which showed focal/multifocal FDG uptake in the myocardium as well as in the lung and intrathoracic and abdominal lymph nodes, suggestive of active myocardial and systemic sarcoidosis. The patient underwent placement of an implantable cardiac defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death. He was discharged receiving guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and started receiving prednisone with plans for a prolonged taper for active systemic and cardiac sarcoidosis. In the outpatient setting, he underwent genetic testing for ARVC, which was negative for a pathogenic mutation.

case_info.explanation: B. Cardiac positron emission tomography Several ECG features suggest a diagnosis of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) in this case. There is a notable low-amplitude, positive deflection between the end of the QRS complex and the onset of the T wave, most prominent in the right precordial leads (V2 and V3), consistent with an epsilon wave. Other findings include both premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with a left bundle branch block (LBBB) morphology and an inferior axis. T-wave inversions are seen in leads V1-V4, though notably in the presence of a complete right bundle branch block (cRBBB). The patient met diagnostic criteria for ARVC based on electrophysiological data alone: 1 major criterion, ie, presence of epsilon waves on the ECGs, and 3 minor criteria including T-wave inversions in V1-V4 in the presence of cRBBB, frequent PVCs (>500 per 24 hours on telemetry), as well as nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with an LBBB morphology.1The diagnosis of ARVC was further supported by major imaging criteria as cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed RV regional akinesis and dyskinesis, RV end diastolic volume more than 110 mL/m2, and a moderately decreased systolic function with ejection fraction of 40% or less.1Notably, there was also significant LV involvement with late gadolinium enhancement composing 38% of total LV myocardial mass. However, this finding does not necessarily raise doubt with respect to a diagnosis of ARVC, as concomitant involvement of the left ventricle is a well-documented feature of advanced ARVC, with 1 study documenting LV involvement in 76% of hearts with autopsy-proven ARVC.2 Despite meeting diagnostic criteria for ARVC, there was considerable debate about the underlying pathology given the initial ECG with a “normal” first beat, in which the absence of cRBBB was accompanied by disappearance of T-wave inversion in lead V1 (Figure 1A). In other words, T-wave inversion seen in the right precordial leads, the most frequent ECG abnormality observed in ARVC,1may simply be secondary to conduction delay from cRBBB in the present case. Additionally, although the presence of epsilon waves in the right precordial leads is a major diagnostic criterion, this finding alone is not pathognomonic of ARVC. Discharge home after implantation of implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (choice A) would also be incorrect at this point because the medical management of ARVC and cardiac sarcoidosis is considerably different. The patient underwent placement of an implantable cardiac defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death. He was discharged receiving guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and started receiving prednisone with plans for a prolonged taper for active systemic and cardiac sarcoidosis. In the outpatient setting, he underwent genetic testing for ARVC, which was negative for a pathogenic mutation.

Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: B. Cardiac positron emission tomography Several ECG features suggest a diagnosis of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) in this case. There is a notable low-amplitude, positive deflection between the end of the QRS complex and the onset of the T wave, most prominent in the right precordial leads (V2 and V3), consistent with an epsilon wave. Other findings include both premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with a left bundle branch block (LBBB) morphology and an inferior axis. T-wave inversions are seen in leads V1-V4, though notably in the presence of a complete right bundle branch block (cRBBB). The patient met diagnostic criteria for ARVC based on electrophysiological data alone: 1 major criterion, ie, presence of epsilon waves on the ECGs, and 3 minor criteria including T-wave inversions in V1-V4 in the presence of cRBBB, frequent PVCs (>500 per 24 hours on telemetry), as well as nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with an LBBB morphology.1The diagnosis of ARVC was further supported by major imaging criteria as cardiac magnetic resonance imaging revealed RV regional akinesis and dyskinesis, RV end diastolic volume more than 110 mL/m2, and a moderately decreased systolic function with ejection fraction of 40% or less.1Notably, there was also significant LV involvement with late gadolinium enhancement composing 38% of total LV myocardial mass. However, this finding does not necessarily raise doubt with respect to a diagnosis of ARVC, as concomitant involvement of the left ventricle is a well-documented feature of advanced ARVC, with 1 study documenting LV involvement in 76% of hearts with autopsy-proven ARVC.2 Despite meeting diagnostic criteria for ARVC, there was considerable debate about the underlying pathology given the initial ECG with a “normal” first beat, in which the absence of cRBBB was accompanied by disappearance of T-wave inversion in lead V1 (Figure 1A). In other words, T-wave inversion seen in the right precordial leads, the most frequent ECG abnormality observed in ARVC,1may simply be secondary to conduction delay from cRBBB in the present case. Additionally, although the presence of epsilon waves in the right precordial leads is a major diagnostic criterion, this finding alone is not pathognomonic of ARVC. An epsilon wave is an electrical marker of delayed activation of the right ventricular free wall and outflow tract and can be seen in association with other cardiac pathologies that involve the right ventricle such as myocardial infarction and sarcoidosis.3Myocarditis may also be associated with epsilon waves,4though this patient’s inflammatory markers including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were undetectably low, strongly favoring against active myocarditis. With regard to the best next step in management, an echocardiogram is limited in its ability to definitively evaluate for major imaging features necessary to discern a diagnosis of ARVC vs cardiac sarcoidosis (choice C). An electrophysiology study would be premature and unlikely to aid in establishing an etiology (choice D). Discharge home after implantation of implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (choice A) would also be incorrect at this point because the medical management of ARVC and cardiac sarcoidosis is considerably different. Cardiac 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (Figure 2) scan was obtained (choice B), which showed focal/multifocal FDG uptake in the myocardium as well as in the lung and intrathoracic and abdominal lymph nodes, suggestive of active myocardial and systemic sarcoidosis. The patient underwent placement of an implantable cardiac defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death. He was discharged receiving guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and started receiving prednisone with plans for a prolonged taper for active systemic and cardiac sarcoidosis. In the outpatient setting, he underwent genetic testing for ARVC, which was negative for a pathogenic mutation.

messages.content:
You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his mid-50s with a medical history of nonspecific T-wave abnormalities on electrocardiogram (ECG) reported new-onset chest discomfort, diaphoresis, and shortness of breath that woke him from sleep. Emergency medical services found him to be in a wide complex tachycardia. He was administered a 150-mg bolus of intravenous amiodarone, which failed to terminate his arrhythmia. He ultimately required synchronized cardioversion with a biphasic direct current shock of 100 J. On arrival to the emergency department, his vital signs were stable. Serum electrolyte levels were within normal range and C-reactive protein was less than 6 mg/dL (to convert to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10). High-sensitivity troponin peaked at 1078 pg/mL. His initial 12-lead ECG is shown inFigure 1A. He continued in sinus rhythm with episodes of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia observed on telemetry, as shown inFigure 1B. Cardiac catheterization revealed patent coronary arteries. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was remarkable for a dilated right ventricle with moderately reduced systolic function and transmural late gadolinium enhancement with akinesis and dyskinesis involving the right ventricular (RV) free wall and outflow tract extending to the left ventricular (LV) anterior, septal, and apical segments.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Given the patient's significant cardiac findings, including dilated right ventricle, reduced systolic function, and prior episodes of ventricular tachycardia, the most appropriate next step in management is option A: Discharge home after implantation of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD). The presence of high troponin levels alongside these structural changes indicates a risk for life-threatening arrhythmias, justifying the need for ICD placement to prevent sudden cardiac death.

I agree that an ICD is likely indicated, but I'd like to clarify the diagnosis first. The combination of RV/LV involvement with transmural LGE and ventricular arrhythmias in a patient with normal coronaries strongly points to cardiac sarcoidosis or another infiltrative cardiomyopathy. Discharging immediately after ICD placement without confirming the underlying etiology and starting targeted immunosuppressive therapy could leave a reversible condition untreated.

You raise a pertinent point about the need for further diagnostic workup. A transthoracic echocardiogram (option C) can provide additional information regarding the left ventricular function and structure, which may help clarify the etiology of the patient's cardiomyopathy and guide further management. After this assessment, we can make a more informed decision regarding ICD placement and any necessary treatment for an underlying condition.

An echocardiogram has largely been superseded by the detailed CMR findings already provided, which show specific RV/LV involvement and transmural LGE. The critical next step is to pursue a tissue diagnosis, such as an endomyocardial biopsy, to confirm suspected cardiac sarcoidosis or another infiltrative process, as this directly dictates the need for immunosuppression alongside device therapy.

I appreciate your emphasis on the need for a tissue diagnosis. Given the potential for a reversible condition such as cardiac sarcoidosis, I agree that an electrophysiology study (option D) to investigate further and possibly obtain a biopsy is warranted before proceeding with ICD implantation. This will provide clarity on the underlying pathology and guide our management more effectively.

That's a sound plan. An electrophysiology study with endomyocardial biopsy would be the definitive next step to confirm cardiac sarcoidosis or another infiltrative disease, as this directly impacts whether to initiate immunosuppressive therapy in conjunction with ICD placement for secondary prevention.

I concur that an electrophysiology study is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis of cardiac sarcoidosis or another infiltrative condition before proceeding with ICD implantation. This approach ensures we address any reversible pathology effectively and tailor our management accordingly.

Excellent. We can then proceed with ICD for secondary prevention and initiate targeted immunosuppression if sarcoidosis is confirmed.

This approach will allow us to tailor our management effectively based on the findings.
